claims.text: The as-cast alloy is a random solid solution with significant compositional disorder.
Controlled thermal annealing can induce nanoscale short-range chemical ordering.
The proposed annealing regime can promote partial ordering without producing secondary phases or significant grain growth.
Annealing-induced short-range ordered clusters reduce local chemical inhomogeneity.
Partial chemical ordering reduces electron scattering caused by compositional disorder.
Reduced disorder-induced electron scattering enhances the effective Cooper-pairing interaction within a conventional BCS mechanism.
Chemical and structural disorder can cause different regions of a superconductor to transition at different temperatures, broadening the specific-heat anomaly.
The unannealed alloy has a lower superconducting transition temperature because of disorder-induced electron scattering.
Annealing-induced partial ordering produces a more uniform superconducting order parameter.
Annealed samples will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit a narrower and sharper specific-heat jump at the superconducting transition than as-cast samples.
A sharper specific-heat transition indicates greater superconducting homogeneity.
The proposed mechanism applies only while annealing produces nanoscale ordering without secondary phases, macroscopic phase separation, or substantial grain growth.
Excessive annealing may cause macroscopic phase separation.
The quantitative increase in Tc and narrowing of the transition are not specified and may be offset by adverse effects of ordering.
The hypothesis is falsified if properly annealed samples lacking secondary phases do not show a statistically significant increase in Tc and sharpening of the transition relative to as-cast controls.
Observation of excessive ordering or secondary phases is itself treated as falsification of the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Secondary-phase formation and excessive ordering are defined as conditions outside the hypothesis's applicability window, but the falsification rule also treats their occurrence as falsifying the mechanism. Such observations would instead show that the intended intervention was not achieved unless a separate in-window treatment condition had been verified.
